title: Music Theory
subtitle: Notes, scales, chords and harmony from the ground up, with Python labs, an ear trainer and a circle of fifths
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A beginner-friendly course in Western music theory: pitch and notes, reading the staff and rhythm, intervals, major and minor scales and modes, key signatures, triads and seventh chords, inversions, Roman numeral harmony and cadences, melody, form, transposition and writing a simple song. Python labs build scales and chords from numbers; an interactive ear trainer and a circle of fifths let you hear and see the ideas.

chapters.title: Sound, pitch and the notes
summary: Sound is vibration. How fast something vibrates, its frequency in hertz (Hz), sets the pitch. A faster vibration sounds higher.
Western music divides the octave, a doubling of frequency, into twelve equal steps called semitones. The seven white keys on a piano are the notes A to G, and the black keys are sharps or flats.
Each note has a letter name and an octave number, such as C4 for middle C. Concert A, A4, is 440 Hz.

glossary.def: The number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
How high or low a note sounds, set mostly by its frequency.
The interval between a note and the one with double its frequency.
The smallest step in Western music; twelve of them make an octave.
A sign that changes a note by a semitone: sharp (♯), flat (♭) or natural (♮).

keyPoints: Pitch goes up with frequency.
An octave doubles the frequency: A4 = 440 Hz, A5 = 880 Hz.
12 semitones make an octave.
Letter names A B C D E F G, then repeat.
Sharp (♯) raises by one semitone; flat (♭) lowers by one.

items: ELI5. A note is how fast something wiggles. Wiggle twice as fast and you hear the same note, only higher, like a mouse and a bear singing the same song.

Pluck a guitar string and watch it blur. The blur is the string vibrating, many times a second. The more times, the higher the sound. A string that vibrates 440 times a second gives the note A above middle C, the pitch orchestras tune to.

Double the frequency and your ear hears the same note again, only higher. That is the octave. It is why a man and a woman can sing the same tune an octave apart, and why notes in different octaves share a letter name.

Western music cuts the octave into twelve equal steps. Each step is a semitone, and each step multiplies the frequency by the twelfth root of two, about 1.0595. On a piano, neighbouring keys, white or black, are one semitone apart.

The white keys are named A, B, C, D, E, F and G. Between most pairs of white keys sits a black key. It can be named by the note below with a sharp, as in C♯, or by the note above with a flat, as in D♭. The two names mean the same key and are called enharmonic.

There is no black key between B and C, and none between E and F. So B to C and E to F are semitones, while C to D and the other white pairs are two semitones, called a whole tone. This uneven pattern is the key to all scales.

A pitch is named by a letter and an octave number. Middle C is C4. The C above it is C5. Computers number the keys from 0 to 127 in MIDI, where middle C is 60 and A4 is 69. A frequency follows from the MIDI number with one formula: 440 times two to the power of (number minus 69) over twelve.

practice.title: Note to MIDI
practice.intro: Write note_to_midi(name) for names like 'C4', 'F#3' or 'Bb2' (letter, optional # or b, octave). MIDI number = 12 x (octave + 1) + pitch class, where C=0 D=2 E=4 F=5 G=7 A=9 B=11, # adds 1 and b subtracts 1.
practice.hint: Use the table, then adjust for the accidental.

practice.title: MIDI to frequency
practice.intro: Write midi_to_hz(n): 440 x 2 to the power ((n - 69) / 12), rounded to 2 decimals. Use 2 ** x with floats and round(value, 2).
practice.hint: Use the formula directly.
practice.solution:
def midi_to_hz(n):
    return round(440.0 * (2 ** ((n - 69) / 12.0)), 2)

chapters.title: Reading music: staff, clefs and rhythm
summary: Music is written on a staff of five lines and four spaces. A clef at the start says which pitches the lines stand for. The treble clef fixes the second line as G4, and the bass clef fixes the fourth line as F3.
The shape of a note shows how long it lasts. A whole note lasts four beats in 4/4 time, a half note two, a quarter one, an eighth half a beat. Each next shape halves the value before it.
The time signature at the start tells how many beats are in each measure and which note gets the beat. In 3/4 there are three quarter-note beats per measure.

glossary.def: Five horizontal lines on which notes are written.
A sign at the start of the staff that fixes the pitch of the lines.
A group of beats between two bar lines.
Two numbers: beats per measure over the note value that gets one beat.
A sign for a silence of a given length.

keyPoints: Treble clef: lines E G B D F; spaces F A C E.
Bass clef: lines G B D F A; spaces A C E G.
Whole = 4 beats, half = 2, quarter = 1, eighth = 1/2 (in 4/4).
A dot adds half the note's value.
Time signature 4/4: four quarter beats per measure.

items: ELI5. Music is written on a ladder with five rungs. Each shape of a note says how long to hold it, like a short or a long step.

The staff is a ladder. Every line and space is one step of the ladder. A note high on the ladder sounds high. A clef is a key to the ladder: it tells you which pitch a certain line means, and the rest follow in order.

In the treble clef, the line curled by the clef is G4. The lines from bottom to top are E, G, B, D, F, and the spaces are F, A, C, E. A rhyme helps: every good boy does fine for the lines, and FACE for the spaces. Notes above and below the staff sit on short ledger lines.

Duration is shown by shape. A hollow oval with no stem is a whole note. Add a stem and it is a half note. Fill the oval and it is a quarter note. Add a flag and it is an eighth note. Each shape lasts half as long as the one before. A dot after a note adds half its length.

Beats are grouped into measures. The time signature 4/4 says four quarter notes in each measure, and 3/4 says three. In 6/8 there are six eighth notes, usually felt as two groups of three. The top number counts beats and the bottom shows the unit.

A rest is silence with a length. It has a shape for every note value, so a whole rest, half rest and so on. In 4/4, a quarter note, a quarter rest and a half note add up to four beats, filling exactly one measure.

practice.title: Measure length
practice.intro: Notes are given as strings: 'w' whole (4 beats), 'h' half (2), 'q' quarter (1), 'e' eighth (0.5), 's' sixteenth (0.25). A trailing '.' adds half again ('h.' is 3). Write measure_beats(notes): the total beats of the list.

chapters.title: Intervals

maps.title: Intervals
links: Perfect | marks | Unison fourth fifth octave
Major | is | One semitone above minor

summary: An interval is the distance between two notes. It has a number, counted in letter names (C up to E is a third), and a quality, found from the semitones (major, minor, perfect, augmented or diminished).
Unisons, fourths, fifths and octaves come in a perfect quality. Seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths come in major and minor.
Learn the intervals by their semitone count and by a familiar song to hear them.

glossary.def: The distance between two notes.
Unison, fourth, fifth or octave in their normal size.
The two normal sizes of seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths; minor is a semitone smaller.
An interval of six semitones, halfway through the octave.
Moving the lower note up an octave; intervals of n and 9 - n then swap.

keyPoints: 0 unison, 1 minor 2nd, 2 major 2nd, 3 minor 3rd, 4 major 3rd.
5 perfect 4th, 6 tritone, 7 perfect 5th.
8 minor 6th, 9 major 6th, 10 minor 7th, 11 major 7th, 12 octave.
Invert: 2nd and 7th, 3rd and 6th, 4th and 5th swap.
Perfect inverts to perfect; major to minor.

items: ELI5. The distance between two notes has a name, like a short hop or a big leap. You learn the hops by tunes you already know.

To find an interval, count letter names from the lower note to the upper one, counting both ends. C to E is C, D, E, which is a third. C to G is a fifth. Then count semitones to find the quality. C to E is 4 semitones, which is a major third. C to E-flat is 3, which is a minor third.

Fourths, fifths and octaves are called perfect because they sound pure and stable. A perfect fifth is 7 semitones, a perfect fourth is 5, and an octave is 12. Make one a semitone bigger and it is augmented, a semitone smaller and it is diminished.

Seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths are major or minor. The minor is one semitone smaller than the major. A major second is 2 semitones, a minor second 1. A major third is 4, a minor third 3. A major sixth is 9, a minor sixth 8. A major seventh is 11, a minor seventh 10.

Six semitones, halfway through the octave, is the tritone. It is either an augmented fourth or a diminished fifth. It sounds tense and wants to resolve, and was nicknamed the devil in music by medieval writers.

Turn an interval upside down by moving the lower note up an octave. The inversion of a third is a sixth, and of a fourth is a fifth. The numbers always add to nine, and the semitones to twelve. Perfect stays perfect, while major becomes minor.

Songs make useful anchors. The first two notes of the Star Wars theme is a perfect fifth. A major third is the start of 'When the Saints Go Marching In'. A minor second is the shark theme from Jaws. Pick your own song for each interval.

chapters.title: Major scales and key signatures

maps.title: Major scales
links: Major scale | follows | W W H W W W H
Key signature | lists | Sharps or flats
Circle of fifths | orders | The keys

summary: A scale is a ladder of notes. The major scale follows the step pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. Starting on C and playing only white keys gives C major.
The first note of a scale is the tonic, the home note that gives the key its name. Each scale degree has a name: tonic, supertonic, mediant, subdominant, dominant, submediant and leading tone.
To play a major scale from any note, apply the same pattern. This forces some notes to be sharp or flat, and these are listed in the key signature.

glossary.def: A set of notes arranged by pitch, such as the major scale.
The first and most important note of a key.
The sharps or flats at the start of the staff that apply to the whole piece.
A diagram of the keys ordered by fifths, showing how many sharps or flats each has.
The minor key that shares a key signature with a major key, starting on its sixth degree.

keyPoints: Major scale pattern: W W H W W W H.
Sharps in order: F C G D A E B.
Flats in order: B E A D G C F.
Up a fifth: add one sharp; down a fifth: add one flat.
Relative minor starts on the sixth degree.

items: ELI5. A scale is a staircase with a pattern of big and small steps. Start on a different step and you must bend a few notes to keep the pattern.

A major scale sounds like do re mi fa so la ti do. The gaps between its notes follow a pattern of whole tones (W, two semitones) and half tones (H, one semitone): W W H W W W H. Start on C and you get all white keys, because the half steps fall at E to F and B to C.

Start on G and apply the same pattern. The step from E to F would be wrong. The pattern needs a whole tone from E up to F-sharp, so F must be raised. G major has one sharp, F-sharp. This is how key signatures arise: they fix the pattern for each starting note.

The sharps appear in a fixed order: F, C, G, D, A, E, B. Each new sharp key is a fifth above the last: C, G, D, A, E, B, F-sharp. The flats come in the reverse order: B, E, A, D, G, C, F. Each new flat key is a fifth below: F, B-flat, E-flat, A-flat and so on.

Arrange the keys in a circle by fifths and you get the circle of fifths. Going clockwise adds a sharp, going anticlockwise adds a flat. At the bottom the sharp and flat keys meet, since F-sharp major and G-flat major sound the same.

To read a key signature of sharps, take the last sharp and go up a half step: that is the major tonic. With one sharp (F-sharp) the key is G. For flats, the second last flat is the key, and with one flat the key is F. Each major key shares its signature with a relative minor, a minor third below.

practice.title: Circle of fifths
practice.intro: Tap keys on the circle to see the scale, the sharps or flats and the relative minor. Visit 4 different keys to complete this lab.
practice.html: Tap a key on the circle.

practice.title: Match the key
practice.intro: Pair each major key with its key signature.

practice.title: Build a major scale
practice.intro: Write major_scale(tonic): given a tonic as a pitch class number 0 to 11 (C = 0), return the list of 7 pitch classes of the major scale, in order, each 0 to 11. Use the steps 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2 and take each note modulo 12.
practice.hint: Add each step and wrap with modulo 12.
practice.solution:
def major_scale(tonic):
    steps = [2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2]
    scale = [tonic % 12]
    n = tonic
    for s in steps:
        n = n + s
        scale.append(n % 12)
    return scale

practice.title: How many sharps?
practice.intro: Write sharps_in_key(tonic): given a major tonic as pitch class 0 to 11, return the number of sharps (positive) or flats (negative) in its key signature using the circle of fifths: go up in fifths (7 semitones) from C. Positions: C 0, G 1, D 2, A 3, E 4, B 5, F# 6, C# 7 (or Db -5), Ab -4, Eb -3, Bb -2, F -1. Use the table 0:0, 7:1, 2:2, 9:3, 4:4, 11:5, 6:6, 1:-5, 8:-4, 3:-3, 10:-2, 5:-1.
practice.hint: A table lookup works; the keys are just a fifth apart.

practice.title: Relative minor
practice.intro: Write relative_minor(tonic): the pitch class of the relative minor tonic, which is the sixth degree of the major scale: tonic + 9, modulo 12.
practice.hint: A minor third below the major tonic is nine semitones above it.
practice.solution:
def relative_minor(tonic):
    return (tonic + 9) % 12

chapters.title: Minor scales and modes

maps.title: Minor and modes
links: Natural minor | follows | W H W W H W W
Melodic minor | raises | Sixth and seventh going up

summary: The natural minor scale follows the step pattern whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole. It sounds darker than major because of its lowered third, sixth and seventh.
The harmonic minor raises the seventh degree to make a stronger pull to the tonic. The melodic minor raises the sixth and seventh going up and uses natural minor coming down.
A mode is a scale built by starting the major scale on a different degree. The seven modes are Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian and Locrian.

glossary.def: A scale with the pattern W H W W H W W; also called the Aeolian mode.
Natural minor with a raised seventh degree.
A scale that raises the sixth and seventh when ascending.
A scale made by starting a parent scale on a different note.
A five-note scale found in folk, blues and rock music.

keyPoints: Natural minor: W H W W H W W.
Harmonic minor: raise the 7th.
Modes start on degrees 1 to 7 of the major scale: Ionian Dorian Phrygian Lydian Mixolydian Aeolian Locrian.
Major pentatonic: 1 2 3 5 6.
Minor pentatonic: 1 b3 4 5 b7.

items: ELI5. Minor sounds a bit sad because one step in the staircase is lowered. The same notes started from another place give different moods, like colours.

Play the white keys from A to A. That is A natural minor. It uses the same notes as C major but starts on the sixth degree, so A minor is the relative minor of C major. Its third degree is C, a minor third above the tonic, and that minor third gives the scale its sad colour.

Natural minor has no half step leading up to the tonic. That makes the end feel weak. The harmonic minor raises the seventh degree by a semitone, giving a leading tone. In A harmonic minor the G becomes G-sharp. This leaves an awkward gap, an augmented second, between the sixth and seventh degrees.

The melodic minor smooths the gap by raising both the sixth and seventh degrees when going up, F-sharp and G-sharp in A minor. Coming down, it returns to natural minor. Jazz musicians often use the ascending form in both directions.

Every major scale gives seven modes, one for each starting degree. Starting on the 2nd gives Dorian, the 3rd Phrygian, the 4th Lydian, the 5th Mixolydian, the 6th Aeolian and the 7th Locrian. Dorian is minor with a bright sixth. Mixolydian is major with a flat seventh, the sound of a lot of rock.

A pentatonic scale leaves out the notes that clash. Major pentatonic is 1 2 3 5 6, as in C D E G A. Minor pentatonic is 1 flat3 4 5 flat7. With only five notes, every combination sounds good together, which is why guitarists start there.

practice.title: Match the mode
practice.intro: Pair each mode with the degree of the major scale where it starts.

practice.title: Build a minor scale
practice.intro: Write minor_scale(tonic, kind): tonic is a pitch class 0 to 11, kind is 'natural' or 'harmonic'. Return the 7 pitch classes. Natural minor steps are 2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2 from the tonic. Harmonic minor is natural with the seventh note raised by one semitone (mod 12).
practice.hint: Build natural minor first, then adjust the last note.

practice.title: Build a mode
practice.intro: Write mode(tonic, degree): the 7 pitch classes of the mode that starts on the given degree (1 to 7) of the MAJOR scale of the given tonic (pitch class 0 to 11). First build the major scale with steps 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, then rotate it to start from the chosen degree. Return the list.
practice.hint: Rotate the list by degree minus one.
practice.solution:
def mode(tonic, degree):
    steps = [2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2]
    scale = [tonic % 12]
    n = tonic
    for s in steps:
        n = n + s
        scale.append(n % 12)
    out = []
    for i in range(7):
        out.append(scale[(degree - 1 + i) % 7])
    return out

practice.title: Pentatonic
practice.intro: Write pentatonic(tonic, kind): pitch classes of the pentatonic scale. 'major' uses semitone offsets [0, 2, 4, 7, 9] from the tonic and 'minor' uses [0, 3, 5, 7, 10]. Return each as (tonic + offset) % 12.
practice.hint: Pick the offsets, then add the tonic.

chapters.title: Chords: triads

maps.title: Triads
links: Chord | has | Three or more notes
Major triad | is | Major third plus minor third
Minor triad | is | Minor third plus major third

summary: A chord is three or more notes sounded together. The simplest is the triad, made by stacking two thirds on a root: the root, the third and the fifth.
The quality depends on the thirds. A major triad is a major third then a minor third, 4 + 3 semitones. A minor triad is 3 + 4. A diminished triad is 3 + 3, and an augmented triad is 4 + 4.
Building a triad on each degree of a major scale gives three major, three minor and one diminished triad.

glossary.def: Three or more notes played together.
A three-note chord of root, third and fifth.
The note a chord is built on and named after.
Whether a triad is major, minor, diminished or augmented.
Using only the notes of the key.

keyPoints: Major triad: 0 4 7. Minor: 0 3 7.
Diminished: 0 3 6. Augmented: 0 4 8.
In a major key: I ii iii IV V vi vii-dim.
Major chords sound bright; minor chords sound sad.
Chord symbols: C, Cm, Cdim, Caug.

items: ELI5. A chord is notes stacked like blocks, every other note of the scale. Which blocks you pick decides if it sounds happy, sad or tense.

Build a chord by skipping notes. Take C, skip D, take E, skip F, take G. That gives C, E and G, a C major triad. The bottom note is the root, the next the third, the top the fifth. Stacking in thirds is the heart of Western harmony.

The sizes of the two thirds set the colour. Major triad: a major third (4 semitones) below a minor third (3). C E G. Minor triad: swap them, a minor third below a major third. C E-flat G. That single lowered note turns bright to sad.

Two odd triads complete the set. Stack two minor thirds, C E-flat G-flat, and you have a diminished triad, tense and unstable. Stack two major thirds, C E G-sharp, and you have an augmented triad, dreamlike and unsettled.

Now build a triad on every degree of C major using only its own notes. C E G is major. D F A is minor. E G B is minor. F A C is major. G B D is major. A C E is minor. B D F is diminished. The pattern is I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi, vii-diminished. Big letters mean major.

Chord symbols write all this down. C means C major, Cm or C-minus is minor, Cdim is diminished, Caug or C+ is augmented. Guitarists read symbols above the lyrics, and pianists often see them above a melody. In the Nashville system the numbers stand in for any key.

practice.title: Match the triad
practice.intro: Pair each triad quality with its semitone pattern.

practice.title: Build a triad
practice.intro: Write triad(root, quality): root is a pitch class 0 to 11 and quality is 'major', 'minor', 'dim' or 'aug'. Return the three pitch classes [root, third, fifth] mod 12, using the offsets 0 4 7 for major, 0 3 7 minor, 0 3 6 dim, 0 4 8 aug.
practice.hint: Look up the offsets, then add the root.

practice.title: Name the triad
practice.intro: Write triad_quality(a, b, c): given three pitch classes of a triad in root position (root, third, fifth, each 0 to 11), compute the two intervals (b - a) mod 12 and (c - b) mod 12 and return 'major' for 4 and 3, 'minor' for 3 and 4, 'dim' for 3 and 3, 'aug' for 4 and 4, otherwise 'other'.
practice.hint: Two intervals decide the quality.

practice.title: Diatonic triads
practice.intro: Write diatonic_triads(tonic): the qualities of the seven triads built on the degrees of the major scale. The answer does not depend on the tonic: return ['major', 'minor', 'minor', 'major', 'major', 'minor', 'dim']. Compute it yourself by building the scale, stacking thirds from the scale, and naming each triad, then return the list of names.
practice.hint: Take every other scale note, wrapping around the list.
practice.solution:
def diatonic_triads(tonic):
    steps = [2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2]
    scale = [tonic % 12]
    n = tonic
    for s in steps:
        n = n + s
        scale.append(n % 12)
    out = []
    for i in range(7):
        a = scale[i]
        b = scale[(i + 2) % 7]
        c = scale[(i + 4) % 7]
        x = (b - a) % 12
        y = (c - b) % 12
        if x == 4 and y == 3:
            out.append("major")
        elif x == 3 and y == 4:
            out.append("minor")
        else:
            out.append("dim")
    return out

chapters.title: Seventh chords and inversions

maps.title: Seventh chords
links: Seventh chord | adds | A fourth note
Minor seventh | has | Minor third and 7th
First inversion | has | Third in the bass
Slash chord | names | The bass note

summary: A seventh chord adds a note a third above the fifth. Stack three thirds on a root and you have four notes: root, third, fifth and seventh.
The main types are major seventh (0 4 7 11), dominant seventh (0 4 7 10), minor seventh (0 3 7 10) and half-diminished (0 3 6 10). The dominant seventh is the engine of classical and jazz harmony.
An inversion puts a note other than the root in the bass. The chord is the same, only the lowest note changes.

glossary.def: A four-note chord made by stacking three thirds.
A major triad with a minor seventh; the V7 chord.
A voicing of a chord with a note other than the root on the bottom.
Numbers such as 6 and 6/4 that show the inversion of a chord.
A chord symbol like C/E, showing the bass note after a slash.

keyPoints: V7 is a dominant seventh built on the 5th degree.
Root position, first inversion (6), second inversion (6/4).
A triad has 3 positions; a seventh chord has 4.
C/E means a C chord with E in the bass.

items: ELI5. Add one more block on top and the chord gets a richer, spicier flavour. Turn the stack upside down and the notes are the same but the bottom changes.

A triad has three notes, and a seventh chord has four. Take C E G and add the next third above, B, and you have C major seventh. Take the B down to B-flat and you have C7, a dominant seventh. A small change in the top note makes a big change in feel.

The dominant seventh is the most important. Built on the fifth degree of the key, it contains a tritone between its third and seventh. In C, G7 contains B and F, a tritone, and the tension resolves when B moves up to C and F moves down to E. That pull is why V7 leads strongly to I.

Four seventh-chord types cover most music. Major seventh is a major triad with a major seventh, 0 4 7 11, smooth and dreamy. Dominant seventh is a major triad with a minor seventh, 0 4 7 10. Minor seventh is a minor triad with a minor seventh, 0 3 7 10. Half-diminished is 0 3 6 10.

An inversion changes which note is lowest. For C major, C E G is root position, E G C is the first inversion, and G C E is the second inversion. The notes are the same, only the lowest changes. The sound differs a little, and moving the bass smoothly is a main reason to invert.

Inversions are named by the interval above the bass. In figured bass, the first inversion of a triad is 6 and the second is 6/4. Pop music writes a slash chord instead: C/E means C major over an E in the bass. Walking basslines often use slash chords.

What is E G C?
What does C/E mean?

chapters.title: Harmony: progressions and cadences

maps.title: Harmony
links: Roman numeral | names | A chord in a key
Authentic cadence | is | V to I

summary: Roman numerals name chords by the scale degree of their root: I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi and vii-dim in a major key. Big numerals are major chords and small ones are minor, so the same pattern works in every key.
Chords have jobs. The tonic (I) is home. The subdominant (IV, ii) moves away. The dominant (V, vii-dim) creates tension that wants to return home. Common progressions combine these jobs.
A cadence is a chord pair that ends a phrase, like a full stop or a comma. The authentic cadence V to I is a full stop, and the half cadence ending on V is a comma.

glossary.def: Naming chords by the scale degree of their root.
Chords that feel stable and at rest, such as I and vi.
Chords that create tension needing resolution, such as V and vii-dim.
A closing chord pair at the end of a phrase.
A sequence of chords.

keyPoints: I ii iii IV V vi vii-dim.
Tonic: I vi. Subdominant: IV ii. Dominant: V vii.
Authentic cadence V-I, plagal IV-I, half cadence ends on V, deceptive V-vi.
Pop loop: I-V-vi-IV.
Jazz turnaround: ii-V-I.

items: ELI5. Chords tell a little story: leave home, wander, feel the pull, come back. The ending is called a cadence, like a full stop or a comma.

Say we are in the key of C major. The chords are C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am and B-dim. Roman numerals replace those names with degrees, I ii iii IV V vi vii-dim. If the key changes to G, the chords change, but the numerals stay the same. A progression I-IV-V is the same shape in any key.

Chords play roles, like characters in a story. The tonic chord is home: the story starts and ends here. The subdominant steps away, a little restless. The dominant builds tension that wants to go home.
Moving through these roles in the order tonic, subdominant, dominant, tonic is the base of classical and pop harmony.

A cadence is the ending of a phrase. The authentic cadence goes V to I, strong and final, like a full stop. The plagal cadence goes IV to I, the amen at the end of hymns. The half cadence stops on V and feels like a comma.
The deceptive cadence goes V to vi, a surprise that dodges the expected ending.

Some progressions turn up everywhere. I-V-vi-IV drives countless pop songs. I-vi-IV-V is the 1950s doo-wop loop. The twelve-bar blues uses I, IV and V in a fixed pattern. In jazz, ii-V-I is the standard turnaround, resolving down by fifths.

Minor keys work the same way with different chords. In A minor, the harmonic minor scale gives i, ii-dim, III, iv, V, VI and vii-dim. The raised seventh makes V major, so minor keys can still end with a strong V to i cadence. Writing the progression in numerals lets you move it to any key.

options: Creates tension that resolves to I

practice.title: Roman numeral to chord
practice.intro: Write chord_in_key(tonic, numeral): tonic is a pitch class 0 to 11 for a MAJOR key, numeral is one of 'I','ii','iii','IV','V','vi','vii'. Return the three pitch classes of that diatonic triad. Build the major scale, take the degree (I=0 ... vii=6), and stack scale notes at +0, +2 and +4 degrees (wrapping around).
practice.hint: Index into the scale list with wrap-around.
practice.solution:
def chord_in_key(tonic, numeral):
    steps = [2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2]
    scale = [tonic % 12]
    n = tonic
    for s in steps:
        n = n + s
        scale.append(n % 12)
    names = ["I", "ii", "iii", "IV", "V", "vi", "vii"]
    d = names.index(numeral)
    return [scale[d], scale[(d + 2) % 7], scale[(d + 4) % 7]]

practice.title: A progression
practice.intro: Write progression(tonic, numerals): for a list of numerals return a list of the root pitch classes of each chord in the major key tonic (I=degree 0 ... vii=degree 6). For tonic 0 and ['I','V','vi','IV'] the roots are [0, 7, 9, 5].
practice.hint: Reuse the scale and look up each numeral.
practice.solution:
def progression(tonic, numerals):
    steps = [2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2]
    scale = [tonic % 12]
    n = tonic
    for s in steps:
        n = n + s
        scale.append(n % 12)
    names = ["I", "ii", "iii", "IV", "V", "vi", "vii"]
    return [scale[names.index(x)] for x in numerals]

chapters.title: Melody, rhythm and form

maps.title: Melody and form
links: Melody | is | A line of notes

summary: A melody is a line of notes that makes sense as a tune. It is built from motifs, short ideas that are repeated, varied and developed into phrases.
Rhythm gives melody its shape in time. Syncopation puts stress on weak beats, and a groove repeats a pattern.
Form is the large-scale plan. Common forms use letters for sections: AB, ABA, verse and chorus, rondo, theme and variations.

glossary.def: A short musical idea that is repeated and developed.
A musical sentence, usually ending in a cadence.
Stress on a normally weak beat or between beats.
Two-part AB and three-part ABA structures.
Combining independent melodies that fit together.

keyPoints: Motif, phrase, period, section.
A period = antecedent (question) + consequent (answer).
Forms: AB, ABA, rondo ABACA, verse-chorus.
Syncopation: accents off the beat.
Counterpoint: independent lines that make good harmony.

items: ELI5. A tune is a small idea said, repeated and changed. Songs arrange those ideas into sections, like verse and chorus.

Hum Happy Birthday. The first four notes are a motif. The song repeats it, changes it a little and builds a complete phrase. Most tunes work like that: take a small idea, repeat it, change it, and give it a clear ending.

Phrases pair up like questions and answers. The first phrase, the antecedent, ends on an open chord like V. The second phrase, the consequent, answers with a closed ending on I. Together they form a period, the basic sentence of tonal music.

Rhythm decides whether a tune dances. In 4/4, the strong beats are one and three. Place accents on the weaker two and four, or between beats, and you get syncopation, the heart of jazz, funk and Latin music. A pattern that repeats makes a groove.

Form is the architecture. A song with verse and chorus alternates sections, say A B A B. A classical minuet uses ternary form ABA. A rondo returns to its main theme between episodes, ABACA. Theme and variations keep the harmony and change the surface.

Counterpoint means point against point. Two melodies played together, each good by itself, make good harmony together. Bach's fugues are the classic example, where a subject enters in one voice after another. The basic rules are to move mostly in contrary motion and treat parallel fifths with care.

chapters.title: Transposition, ear training and putting it together

maps.title: Putting it together
links: Ear training | learns | Intervals and chords

summary: To transpose a piece, shift every note by the same interval. The pattern of intervals, and therefore the tune, is unchanged, only the pitch level moves.
Ear training links sounds to names. Learn the intervals from songs, sing scale degrees with solfege (do re mi), and hear chord qualities as colours.
Writing a short song uses everything you have learned: pick a key, choose a progression, write a melody that uses chord tones on strong beats, and shape the form.

glossary.def: Moving music up or down by a fixed interval.
Syllables do re mi fa sol la ti used to name scale degrees.
Practice that links sounds with their names.
A note that belongs to the chord sounding at that moment.
A melody with chord symbols above it.

keyPoints: Transpose: add the same number of semitones to each note.
Solfege: do re mi fa sol la ti do.
Hear intervals through songs.
Strong beats: chord tones; weak beats: passing notes.
A lead sheet = melody + chords.

items: ELI5. Moving a song to another key is sliding every note the same distance. It is the same song in a higher or lower voice.

Singers who find a song too high ask to transpose it. Every note moves down by the same number of semitones. The shape and the intervals are the same, so it is still recognisably the same song. Transposing up a whole tone adds two semitones to every note.

Musicians who play in different instruments also transpose. A B-flat clarinet sounds a whole tone lower than written, so its part is written two semitones higher. A key change in a pop song, up a semitone or a tone for the last chorus, is a transposition.

Ear training makes the symbols audible. Sing the scale with solfege: do re mi fa sol la ti do. Learn each interval by a song. Play triads and learn to hear whether they are major or minor. A few minutes a day for a month changes how you hear music.

Now try writing a small song. Pick a key such as C major. Choose a four-chord loop such as I V vi IV. Write a melody where the notes on strong beats are notes of the chord that is sounding, and let notes on weak beats move by step between them. End the phrase on the tonic.

Theory describes what music does. It does not decide what is good. Use it to understand what you like, to find what a piece is doing, and to get ideas when you are stuck. The best next step is to play and listen to music with a theory ear, and to keep notes of what you find.
